newsitem.title: USA: U.S. judge refuses to throw out Healthdyne "pill".
newsitem.headline: U.S. judge refuses to throw out Healthdyne "pill".

text.p: A U.S. District Court judge on Thursday denied a request by Invacare Corp to block a portion of hostile target Healthdyne Technologies Inc's shareholder rights plan, or "poison pill."
In a 13-page decision, U.S. District Court Judge Clarence Cooper ruled, in part, that Invacare had failed to prove it would suffer irreparable harm if the injunction was not issued.
Invacare, which has launched a $200 million bid for Healthdyne, had sought a preliminary injunction to invalidate the portion of the pill known as a "continuing directors", or "deadhand" provision.

The provision essentially prohibits new directors from overturning Healthdyne's poison pill, which has a five percent trigger. Invacare has launched a proxy fight to install its own board slate in order to take control of the company and abolish the posion pill.
Invacare had argued that the Healthdyne provision was illegal.
In his ruling, Cooper noted that Georgia corporate law has supported the concept of continuing directors as a defense strategy against hostile takeover.s
"...The court is satisfied that the concept of continuing directors is an integral part of a takeover defense and is not contrary to public policy in Georgia," he wrote.
Healthdyne is based in Marietta, Ga., Invacare in Elyria, Ohio.

Cooper also denied Invacare's attempt to propose a bylaw that would require the Healthdyne board to eliminate the continuing directors provision. Invacare had wanted shareholders to vote on the bylaw at the July 30 annual meeting.
"Needless to say, we are very pleased with the decision," Healthdyne Chief Executive Craig Reynolds told Reuters.
Invacare Chief Executive Malachi Mixon told Reuters that the company would likely appeal the decision.
